In Ref.1, we argued that a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment in which the Fermilab-NUMI beam in its high-energy mode is aimed at the planned Hyper-Kamiokande detector would be capable of constraining the size of those extra matter effects, provided the vacuum value of \sin^2 2\theta_{23} is not too close to one. In Ref. 1, we argued that a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment, with the Fermilab NuMI beam operated in its high-energy mode and directed toward the planned Hyper-Kamiokande detector, would be capable of constraining the magnitude of these additional matter effects, provided that the vacuum value of \(\sin^2 2\theta_{23}\) is not too close to unity. outputs.L2: Physics beyond the Standard Model may produce additional matter-induced effects in neutrino oscillations, if the associated new interactions treat the three neutrino flavors differently. In Ref. 1, we showed that a long-baseline oscillation experiment using the Fermilab NUMI beam in high-energy mode, directed toward the proposed Hyper-Kamiokande detector, could place bounds on the magnitude of these extra matter effects, as long as the vacuum value of \(\sin^2 2\theta_{23}\) is not extremely close to unity. New physics beyond the Standard Model could modify the way neutrinos propagate through matter. In the Standard Model, matter effects in neutrino oscillations arise because electron neutrinos interact differently with electrons in ordinary matter than muon or tau neutrinos do. If new particles or interactions exist and couple differently to the three neutrino flavors, they could generate additional flavor-dependent matter effects. These extra contributions would alter the effective neutrino oscillation parameters measured in matter, potentially producing deviations from the expectations based only on vacuum oscillations and Standard Model interactions.

A long-baseline neutrino experiment using the Fermilab-NUMI beam directed toward the Hyper-Kamiokande detector would be well suited to search for, or constrain, such effects. Because neutrinos would travel a very long distance through the Earth before reaching the detector, even small additional matter interactions could accumulate and become observable in the oscillation pattern. By comparing the measured oscillation probabilities with the predictions of standard three-flavor neutrino oscillations, the experiment could place bounds on the size of any nonstandard matter effects.

The sensitivity of this constraint would depend on the true value of the atmospheric mixing angle \(\theta_{23}\). In particular, the constraint would be most effective if the vacuum value of \(\sin^2 2\theta_{23}\) is not too close to one. When \(\sin^2 2\theta_{23}\) is nearly maximal, the oscillation pattern becomes less sensitive to certain new matter-induced shifts, making it harder to distinguish nonstandard interactions from standard oscillation behavior. If the mixing is appreciably nonmaximal, however, deviations caused by new flavor-dependent matter effects would be easier to identify, allowing stronger limits to be set.

Such experimental limits can be translated into constraints on the properties of new particles. If the extra matter effect is produced by the exchange of a new heavy boson, for example, its contribution typically depends on the ratio of the square of its coupling to the square of its mass. Therefore, an upper bound on the size of the nonstandard matter potential can be interpreted as a bound on combinations such as \(g^2/M^2\), where \(g\) is the new interaction strength and \(M\) is the mass of the exchanged particle. For a given coupling strength, the experiment would imply a lower limit on the particle mass; alternatively, for a given mass, it would imply an upper limit on the coupling.

These results would be relevant for a variety of models beyond the Standard Model. One example is topcolor assisted technicolor, in which new gauge interactions and new massive particles may couple nonuniversally to different fermion generations. Such nonuniversal couplings can naturally lead to flavor-dependent neutrino matter effects. Long-baseline neutrino measurements could therefore provide complementary tests of these models, alongside collider searches and precision electroweak measurements. In this way, neutrino oscillation experiments can probe new physics not only through direct detection of neutrino properties, but also through subtle matter-induced effects caused by interactions beyond the Standard Model.

New flavor-dependent interactions beyond the Standard Model may modify the way neutrinos propagate through matter. In ordinary three-flavor neutrino oscillations, matter effects arise from the standard charged-current interaction of electron neutrinos with electrons in the Earth. If additional interactions exist, for example interactions that distinguish between neutrino flavors, they can generate extra effective matter potentials. These nonstandard matter effects would change the oscillation probabilities measured in long-baseline experiments and could therefore be tested by precision neutrino beams.

This study considers the sensitivity of a long-baseline experiment using the Fermilab NuMI high-energy neutrino beam directed toward a large water-Cherenkov detector such as Hyper-Kamiokande. Because the beam would travel a very long distance through the Earth before reaching the detector, matter effects would be enhanced, making the setup especially useful for probing small flavor-dependent deviations from the Standard Model. The analysis focuses on how such new interactions would affect the disappearance and appearance channels of atmospheric-scale neutrino oscillations, particularly through modifications of the effective mixing involving \(\nu_\mu\) and \(\nu_\tau\).

The strength of these new matter effects can be described phenomenologically by parameters that measure the difference between the forward-scattering potentials of different neutrino flavors. If no deviation from the Standard Model oscillation pattern is observed, the experiment can place bounds on these parameters. The sensitivity is especially strong when the vacuum value of \(\sin^2 2\theta_{23}\) is not extremely close to one. In that case, the oscillation probability is more easily distorted by additional matter potentials, and the degeneracy between maximal mixing and new physics effects is reduced.

The resulting constraints can also be interpreted in terms of specific particle-physics models. In models such as topcolor assisted technicolor, new heavy gauge bosons or other particles can induce flavor-dependent neutrino interactions with matter. The experimental bounds on the effective matter-potential parameters can therefore be translated into limits on combinations of the new coupling constants and mediator masses. Roughly speaking, stronger limits on the nonstandard interaction parameters imply that either the new particles must be heavier, their couplings to ordinary matter and neutrinos must be weaker, or both.

Thus, a Fermilab-to-Hyper-Kamiokande high-energy long-baseline experiment would not only measure standard oscillation parameters but also provide a sensitive test of new flavor-dependent forces. Its ability to constrain such interactions would complement searches at colliders and other precision experiments, offering an indirect probe of new physics at energy scales beyond those directly accessible in neutrino oscillation experiments.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a particle physics talk about using a Fermilab NUMI high-energy beam aimed at Hyper-Kamiokande to constrain nonstandard neutrino matter effects and relate them to topcolor-assisted technicolor models.
counterfactuals.output: We discuss the sensitivity of a hypothetical Fermilab NuMI high-energy neutrino beam directed toward Hyper-Kamiokande to nonstandard neutrino interactions in matter. The very long baseline and broad energy spectrum provide enhanced sensitivity to matter-induced modifications of oscillation probabilities, allowing constraints on effective NSI parameters that are complementary to conventional long-baseline and atmospheric measurements. We focus on flavor-changing and nonuniversal matter effects, examining their impact on appearance and disappearance channels and their correlations with standard oscillation parameters, including the mass ordering and CP phase. The resulting bounds are interpreted in the context of topcolor-assisted technicolor models, where new neutral gauge bosons can generate effective neutrino–matter couplings. This connection illustrates how precision neutrino oscillation data can probe TeV-scale dynamics associated with electroweak symmetry breaking and fermion mass generation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize how long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments can test new flavor-dependent interactions beyond the Standard Model, mentioning sin^2 2θ23, extra matter effects, and limits on new particle masses and couplings.
counterfactuals.output:
Long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments test for new flavor-dependent interactions by sending neutrinos over hundreds to thousands of kilometers and comparing the observed flavor transitions with Standard Model oscillation predictions.

A key observable is the atmospheric mixing parameter, often written as **sin²2θ₂₃**, which controls the strength of **νμ disappearance** and **νμ → ντ/νe appearance**. If new flavor-dependent forces exist, they can modify the effective oscillation pattern, shifting the measured value of sin²2θ₂₃ or producing apparent differences between neutrino and antineutrino oscillations.

Such new interactions can also create **extra matter effects** as neutrinos travel through Earth. In the Standard Model, electron neutrinos experience the usual charged-current matter potential from electrons. New flavor-dependent interactions would add additional effective potentials, depending on the neutrino flavor and the composition of matter. These nonstandard matter effects can change oscillation probabilities, energy spectra, and baseline dependence, making long-baseline experiments especially sensitive.

By looking for deviations from the expected oscillation behavior, experiments can place limits on the strength of these new interactions. These bounds are often expressed as constraints on:

- **new couplings**, describing how strongly a new force couples to different neutrino flavors or to matter particles;
- **new mediator masses**, such as hypothetical gauge bosons or scalar particles that carry the interaction;
- combinations like **coupling divided by mediator mass**, since low-energy oscillation experiments typically probe an effective interaction strength proportional to something like \(g^2/M^2\).

If no anomalous matter effect or distortion of sin²2θ₂₃ is observed, long-baseline data can exclude regions of parameter space for new flavor-dependent forces, setting lower limits on mediator masses for a given coupling, or upper limits on couplings for a given mass. Thus, precision measurements of neutrino oscillations provide a sensitive indirect probe of physics beyond the Standard Model.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a conference-style paragraph explaining the result of a previous paper on nonstandard neutrino interactions at a NUMI-to-Hyper-K experiment and what will be discussed in the present talk.
counterfactuals.output: In a previous study, we investigated the physics potential of a NuMI-to-Hyper-Kamiokande configuration for probing nonstandard neutrino interactions (NSI) during long-baseline propagation. The analysis showed that the very long baseline and high-statistics Hyper-K detector would make this setup particularly sensitive to matter-induced effects, allowing it to test flavor-changing NSI parameters—especially those involving the electron sector—at levels competitive with, and in some regions complementary to, other next-generation oscillation facilities. It was also found that NSI can introduce important degeneracies with the standard oscillation parameters, notably the leptonic CP-violating phase and the neutrino mass ordering, thereby affecting the interpretation of appearance-channel measurements. In this talk, I will summarize the main conclusions of that work, discuss the origin of the relevant NSI effects in the oscillation probabilities, and present the expected sensitivity of the NuMI-to-Hyper-K setup to NSI parameters. I will also comment on parameter degeneracies, correlations with standard three-flavor oscillation physics, and the role such a configuration could play in the broader global program to search for physics beyond the standard neutrino oscillation framework.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an abstract for a research presentation on beyond-Standard-Model matter effects in neutrino oscillations, focusing on the Fermilab NuMI beam, Hyper-Kamiokande, and implications for topcolor assisted technicolor.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Neutrino oscillation experiments provide a sensitive probe of physics beyond the Standard Model through possible nonstandard matter effects that modify neutrino propagation in matter. In this presentation, we investigate the phenomenology of beyond-Standard-Model matter interactions in long-baseline oscillation experiments, with particular emphasis on the Fermilab NuMI beam program and the future Hyper-Kamiokande experiment. We parameterize new matter effects in terms of effective neutral-current-like interactions between neutrinos and ambient fermions, and study their impact on oscillation probabilities, event spectra, and the extraction of standard oscillation parameters such as the CP-violating phase, the atmospheric mixing angle, and the neutrino mass ordering.

The NuMI beam, with its established long-baseline configurations and sensitivity to matter-enhanced oscillation effects, offers an important testing ground for subleading deviations from the standard three-flavor framework. Hyper-Kamiokande, with its high statistics, broad physics reach, and sensitivity to both accelerator and atmospheric neutrinos, will significantly improve constraints on such new interactions and help resolve degeneracies between standard CP violation and exotic matter-induced effects. We discuss how combined analyses of NuMI-based data and Hyper-Kamiokande measurements can distinguish genuine leptonic CP violation from new matter effects and can place competitive bounds on flavor-changing and nonuniversal neutrino interactions.

Finally, we explore the implications of these constraints for topcolor assisted technicolor models, in which new strong dynamics and extended gauge sectors may induce effective neutrino-matter interactions at low energies. We identify regions of parameter space where such models could generate observable deviations in long-baseline oscillation experiments, while remaining consistent with current electroweak and flavor constraints. These results highlight the complementarity of precision neutrino oscillation measurements and collider or low-energy probes in testing dynamical electroweak symmetry breaking scenarios.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal high-energy physics language, describe a talk about constraining flavor-dependent new physics through long-baseline neutrino oscillations and translating those constraints into bounds on couplings and masses of new particles.
counterfactuals.output:
This talk presents a phenomenological study of flavor-dependent new physics in the neutrino sector using precision long-baseline oscillation data. We formulate possible beyond-the-Standard-Model effects in terms of effective interactions that modify neutrino propagation and/or production and detection amplitudes, with particular emphasis on flavor non-universal and flavor-changing structures. Such effects are parametrized at low energies by effective operators or, equivalently, by generalized matter potentials and non-standard interaction coefficients.

Using long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, where matter effects, baseline dependence, and energy spectra provide sensitivity to flavor-dependent distortions of the oscillation probability, we derive constraints on the relevant new-physics parameters. The analysis exploits appearance and disappearance channels, including correlations with the standard oscillation parameters, the leptonic CP-violating phase, and the neutrino mass ordering. Special attention is given to degeneracies between standard three-flavor oscillation effects and new flavor structures, as well as to the role of near-detector information and spectral measurements in lifting these degeneracies.

The resulting bounds on effective interaction coefficients are then interpreted in ultraviolet-motivated scenarios. In particular, we translate the oscillation limits into constraints on the masses and couplings of hypothetical mediators, such as new neutral gauge bosons, scalar mediators, or leptoquark-like states that generate flavor-dependent neutrino interactions after being integrated out. For a mediator of mass \(M\) and coupling \(g\), the effective scale is schematically constrained through combinations of the form  
\[
\epsilon_{\alpha\beta} \sim \frac{g_\alpha g_\beta}{2\sqrt{2}G_F M^2},
\]
allowing oscillation data to be recast as exclusion regions in the \((g,M)\) plane.

The talk emphasizes the complementarity between long-baseline oscillation experiments and other probes of new physics, including charged-lepton flavor violation, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, collider searches, and precision electroweak measurements. While oscillation experiments are primarily sensitive to flavor structure and matter-induced effects rather than directly to high mass scales, their ability to probe extremely small flavor-dependent potentials makes them a powerful indirect tool for testing new physics coupled to neutrinos.

Overall, the presentation demonstrates how long-baseline neutrino data can be used not only to constrain deviations from the standard three-flavor oscillation paradigm, but also to place quantitative limits on the couplings and masses of new particles in well-defined beyond-the-Standard-Model frameworks.
